106.title: The eleven blessings
106.hook: sleep well, wake well, no bad dreams, dear to people and to other beings
106.howItsDone: Some Buddhists practice or chant metta before sleep, and the eleven benefits from the Anguttara Nikaya are recited in teachings and on protective chanting occasions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: karaniya, the metta sutta, and a mother protecting her only child. Your line: as a mother.

It's midnight. You're in bed, and your mind is replaying an argument from this afternoon. What you said. What you should have said. What you'll say next time. Your heart is going a little fast. Sleep isn't coming. The clock says twelve-forty, then one-fifteen. Today's text makes a promise that sounds surprisingly modern. It's a short list from the Anguttara Nikaya, the collection of numbered teachings, and the very first thing on it is this: a person who practices loving-kindness sleeps well.
screen: `MIDNIGHT, REPLAYING THE ARGUMENT.` → `SLEEP ISN'T COMING.` → `THE FIRST BLESSING: SLEEP WELL.`

segments.voice: The text is called the Metta Sutta too, a different one, in the Book of Elevens. The Buddha lists eleven benefits for someone who practices metta often and well. One, you sleep well. Two, you wake well. Three, you don't have bad dreams. Four, you're dear to people. Five, you're dear to non-human beings, which the tradition understands as spirits and other unseen beings. Six, the gods protect you. Seven, fire, poison and weapons don't harm you. Eight, your mind settles quickly into concentration. Nine, your face is bright and clear. Ten, you die without confusion. And eleven, if you go no further on the path, you're reborn in a heavenly realm, the Brahma world. Different Buddhists hear a list like that in different ways. Some take all eleven at face value, including protection from fire and weapons, and chant metta for protection. Others hear the first few especially as plain observations: it isn't hard to see why a mind that isn't nursing grudges would sleep better, or why people warm to someone who warms to them. The text itself doesn't explain; it lists. But notice where it starts: not with enlightenment, not with the heavens. With sleep, the most ordinary place in your life. And that closes ten days of metta: four phrases, yourself, a benefactor, a friend, a stranger, a difficult person, the barriers broken, all beings, the sutta, and now its blessings. Tomorrow the path turns to the breath.

segments.voice: This practice is made for bedtime, but it works now too: let the body get heavy and the breath slow, then bring to mind anyone from today, the pleasant and the difficult, one at a time, and offer each a single wish: may you be at ease. Let each one go, like closing doors softly down a hallway. Finish with yourself: may I be at ease.

Your line: kindness sleeps well. The first of eleven blessings is the most ordinary one. That's a hundred and six days.

107.title: Sixteen steps
107.hook: the breathing discourse gives sixteen steps in four groups of four
107.howItsDone: Anapanasati is taught in Theravada monasteries and in meditation centers in many countries, and practice begins with simply knowing the in-breath and the out-breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Anguttara Nikaya's eleven blessings, starting with sleep. Your line: kindness sleeps well. Today, ten days with the breath begin.

Since you woke up this morning, you've breathed thousands of times, and you didn't have to think about a single one. Breathing happens whether you pay attention or not. And it only ever happens now. You can't take yesterday's breath, or tomorrow's. Maybe that's why the Pali texts give it a discourse of its own: number 118 in the Middle Length Discourses, the Anapanasati Sutta. It takes something you do without thinking and turns it into a whole path, in sixteen steps.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF BREATHS SINCE MORNING.` → `ONLY EVER NOW.` → `A WHOLE PATH IN SIXTEEN STEPS.`

segments.voice: The discourse opens on a full-moon night at the end of the rainy season. Many monks are gathered, and the Buddha is so pleased with them that he stays another month. Then he teaches this. The standard explanation splits today's word, anapanasati, in three. Ana: breathing in. Apana: breathing out. Sati: mindfulness. It begins simply. A person goes to a forest, the foot of a tree, or an empty room. Sits down, legs crossed, body upright, and sets mindfulness in front. Mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out. Then come sixteen steps, in four groups of four. The first four are about the body: the long breath, the short breath, the whole body, calming the body. The second four, feeling: joy, ease, noticing feelings, calming them. The third four, the mind: knowing it, gladdening it, steadying it, freeing it. The last four, seeing clearly: change, fading, ending, letting go. Body, feeling, mind, and the way things are: a map of the whole inner life, riding on one breath. And the discourse makes a big claim: this simple practice, developed and made much of, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness, and those lead on to awakening. Over the next ten days you'll walk these steps a few at a time. They aren't meant to be finished in a week. But every one begins where you already are: breathing in, breathing out.

segments.voice: Sit the way the discourse describes, as best you can: upright but not stiff, chair or cushion, attention resting where the breath is easiest to feel, the nostrils, the upper lip or the chest. Don't change the breath, just know it: breathing in, you know you're breathing in; breathing out, you know you're breathing out. When the mind wanders, and it will, come back to the next breath.

Your line: sixteen steps, one breath. The whole path fits inside something you already do. Day one hundred and seven, done.

108.title: Long and short
108.hook: steps one and two: a long breath known as long, a short breath as short
108.howItsDone: Buddhist breath meditation usually begins with simply knowing the breath as long or short, as the discourse describes, without controlling it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing, in sixteen steps. Your line: sixteen steps, one breath. Today, step one.

Most breathing advice tells you to do something. Breathe in for four, hold for seven. Belly breathing. Box breathing. Deep breaths before the presentation. Those have their uses. But the first step of the Buddhist breathing discourse is stranger, and harder. It doesn't ask you to change anything: not the length, not the rhythm, not the depth. It asks you to notice. And anyone who has tried it for sixty seconds knows how hard that is.
screen: `IN FOR FOUR, HOLD FOR SEVEN.` → `CHANGE NOTHING.` → `JUST NOTICE.`

segments.voice: Here are steps one and two, from the Middle Length Discourses. Breathing in long, a person knows: I breathe in long. Breathing out long, they know: I breathe out long. Breathing in short, they know it's short; breathing out short, the same. No instruction to make the breath long. The breath is whatever it is; your job is to know it. The discourse on the foundations of mindfulness has a lovely picture for this: a skilled wood turner at his lathe, pulling the cord. Making a long pull, he knows it's long. Making a short pull, he knows it's short. No fuss. The knowing sits right alongside the doing. Why start here? Because the moment you watch the breath, you'll notice something funny: you start controlling it. The breath gets stiff and self-conscious, like someone who knows they're being photographed. Step one is learning to watch without grabbing: let the breath breathe itself, and let the knowing come along for the ride. Long and short are useful words because they're simple. Not good or bad, not deep enough, not right. Relaxed breathing tends to be longer; tense breathing, shorter. So you start to notice which one you're in, which tells you how you actually are, before your mind has come up with a story about it. That knowing, without judging and without fixing, is the root of everything that follows.
screen: `BREATHING IN LONG, KNOW IT'S LONG.` · `THE WOOD TURNER'S LONG PULL.` · `WATCH WITHOUT GRABBING.` · `NOT GOOD OR BAD: LONG OR SHORT.` · then, large: `JUST KNOW IT.`

segments.voice: For two minutes or five, let the breath do whatever it does, and on each in-breath and each out-breath, silently notice: long, or short. If you catch yourself controlling it, that's fine: let go, and wait for the next breath to arrive on its own. If you can't tell long from short, just know: breathing in, breathing out.
Long and short. Steps one and two of the breathing discourse: knowing the breath as it is, without changing it.
Your line: just know it. Long or short, the breath is already telling you something. See you tomorrow.

109.title: The whole body
109.hook: steps three and four: sensing the whole body, calming it
109.howItsDone: In Buddhist breath meditation, practitioners move from simply knowing the breath to feeling it through its whole length, or through the whole body, and letting the body grow calm.

segments.voice: Yesterday: long and short, steps one and two, knowing the breath as it is. Your line: just know it.

Right now, without moving, notice your shoulders. Are they up near your ears? Now your jaw. Is it clenched? Your forehead. Your hands. Is any of them holding on for no reason at all? It's easy to carry a body around all day like a bag you've forgotten you're holding. Steps three and four of the breathing discourse bring the body back into the picture. First, feel all of it. Then, let it settle.
screen: `SHOULDERS UP NEAR YOUR EARS?` → `A BAG YOU FORGOT YOU'RE HOLDING.` → `FEEL ALL OF IT. LET IT SETTLE.`

segments.voice: Notice a small shift in the words. Steps one and two said: a person knows. Steps three and four say: a person trains. Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe in; experiencing the whole body, I will breathe out. Then: calming the body's activity, I will breathe in and out. Knowing has become training; something is being gently developed now. But what does the whole body mean? Here Buddhists read the text differently, and it's worth knowing both. The Visuddhimagga, the old manual, says it's the body of the breath: you feel each breath from its beginning, through its middle, to its end, the whole length of it, not just the tip. Some modern teachers read it as the physical body: the breath felt everywhere, chest, belly, back, shoulders, the whole body breathing. Both readings are practiced today, and the text itself doesn't settle it. Then step four: calming. In a related discourse, the body's activity is explained as the breath itself. So as you feel the whole body, the breath naturally softens and slows, and the body goes quiet with it. You don't force it. You create the conditions, and the settling happens, like mud sinking to the bottom of a still glass of water. The shoulders come down. The jaw lets go.
screen: `FROM KNOWING TO TRAINING.` · `THE WHOLE BREATH, OR THE WHOLE BODY?` · `CALMING THE BODY'S ACTIVITY.` · `MUD SINKING IN STILL WATER.` · then, large: `THE BODY SETTLES.`

segments.voice: Find the breath, then widen your attention until you feel each one from its very beginning to its very end, and wider still, moving the belly, the chest, the back, the shoulders. On each out-breath, let one place soften: the jaw, then the shoulders, then the hands. Don't force the calm; let the body find its own stillness, breath by breath.
Kaya. Body: steps three and four of the breathing discourse, feeling the whole breath, or the whole body, and letting it calm.
Your line: the body settles. Steps three and four bring it back into the picture. That's day one hundred and nine.

110.title: Joy and ease
110.hook: steps five and six: breathing with gladness, breathing with ease
110.howItsDone: Following these steps, Buddhist meditation teachers encourage students to notice and allow the joy (piti) and ease (sukha) that arise as the mind settles, rather than treating practice as grim effort.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kaya, the whole body, felt and calmed. Your line: the body settles.

Meditation has a reputation a bit like flossing. Good for you, mildly unpleasant, something to get through. So it's a surprise when the Buddhist breathing discourse, at step five, says: breathe with joy. And at step six: breathe with ease. Not grim endurance. Gladness. There's a story behind that, one you already know from camp two. A young man, starving himself in the forest, suddenly remembers a happy afternoon from long ago, and asks himself a question that changes everything.
screen: `MEDITATION AS FLOSSING?` → `BREATHE WITH JOY.` → `A QUESTION THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Remember the rose-apple tree. In the Mahasaccaka Sutta, after he has pushed his body through harsh practice to the edge of death, the Buddha-to-be recalls a day long before: sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree while his father was busy, slipping into a quiet, happy stillness. And he asks: why am I afraid of that pleasure? It has nothing to do with craving or harm. That question turned him toward the middle way. Steps five and six carry the same insight. The person trains: experiencing joy, I will breathe in and out. Experiencing ease, I will breathe in and out. Today's word is piti, joy or rapture: the bright, lifting, sometimes tingling gladness that can arise when the mind settles. Its partner is sukha, a softer happiness, ease, contentment. The Visuddhimagga, the old manual, tells them apart with a picture. A traveler lost in the desert, exhausted, sees a pool of water up ahead: that's piti, the thrill. Then he reaches it, drinks and bathes: that's sukha, the deep ease. Both are welcome; both are part of the path. You don't manufacture these feelings. When the body settles, as in steps three and four, pleasure tends to show up on its own: warmth, lightness, a quiet smile. The practice is to let it in, instead of brushing it off as a distraction. If you've learned to trust only effort and discomfort, that can be the hard part. The discourse trains the other way.
screen: `WHY AM I AFRAID OF THAT PLEASURE?` · `PITI: JOY. SUKHA: EASE.` · `THE POOL SEEN, THE POOL REACHED.` · `LET IT IN.` · then, large: `YOU'RE ALLOWED TO ENJOY IT.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle, then look for anything pleasant, however small: the warmth of your hands, the softness of the out-breath, the quiet in the room, the relief of sitting down. Don't create anything; when you find something already there, let it be felt fully for a breath or two. If nothing seems pleasant, notice what's neutral and easy; that counts too.
Piti. Joy, gladness, the bright lift that can come when the mind settles. Step five of the breath.
Your line: you're allowed to enjoy it. Even the Buddha-to-be had to learn that one. A hundred and ten days now.

111.title: Feeling the mind
111.hook: steps seven and eight: knowing the mind's activity and calming it
111.howItsDone: In breath meditation, Buddhists learn to notice the feeling tone of each moment and the mind's labels, letting the mind's activity calm by knowing it clearly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: piti, joy, and its quieter partner, ease. Your line: you're allowed to enjoy it.

You wake up and something feels off. Nothing has happened yet. No bad email, no argument. But a gray cloud sits over the morning, and by nine o'clock you've decided the day is bad, your job is bad, maybe your life is a bit bad. Then someone makes you laugh at lunch, the cloud's gone, and you can't remember what it was. Moods are like weather: they blow in and blow out. Steps seven and eight of the breathing discourse teach you to watch the weather, and let it calm.
screen: `A GRAY CLOUD OVER THE MORNING.` → `GONE BY LUNCH.` → `MOODS ARE LIKE WEATHER.`

segments.voice: Steps seven and eight close the second group of four, the group about feeling. The person trains: experiencing the mind's activity, I will breathe in and out. Calming the mind's activity, I will breathe in and out. What's the mind's activity? A related discourse, the Culavedalla Sutta, answers: feeling and perception. Feeling here doesn't mean emotion exactly. It's vedana: the basic tone of every moment, pleasant, unpleasant, or neither. Perception is how the mind labels things: that's a threat, that's a friend, that's boring. Together they're the machinery underneath a mood. Something feels slightly unpleasant, the mind labels it, and before you know it, there's a story and a storm. Step seven is watching that machinery run, with the breath as your anchor. There's unpleasant. There's the label. There's the cloud forming. You're not the weather; you're the one watching the sky. Step eight, calming, follows the pattern step four did for the body. You don't argue with the mood or wrestle it down. Knowing it clearly, breath after breath, lets it soften by itself. A storm you're watching is very different from a storm you're lost in. Notice the direction, too. The first four steps were about the body, these four about feeling, and next come four about the mind itself: a map that starts in the most physical place, the breath in your nose, and walks you gently inside.

segments.voice: Ask gently: what's the weather in here, sunny, cloudy, stormy, foggy? Don't fix it; name it, then notice its tone: pleasant, unpleasant, or neither. If a mood is strong, feel where it sits in the body, and let each out-breath be a little softer than the last, watching the cloud move rather than chasing it away.
Vedana. Feeling, the basic tone of pleasant, unpleasant or neither: steps seven and eight, knowing the mind's activity, and letting it calm.
Your line: calm the weather. You're not the weather; you're the one watching the sky. Until tomorrow.

112.title: Gladdening the mind
112.hook: steps nine to twelve: the mind known, gladdened, steadied, set free
112.howItsDone: In breath meditation, Buddhist practitioners learn to recognize the mind's state and respond to it: brightening a heavy mind, gathering a scattered one, and loosening whatever it's gripping.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vedana, feeling the mind, moods as weather, known and calmed. Your line: calm the weather. Today, the end of the week.

A kid on a bike, training wheels just off, wobbling down the sidewalk. A good parent doesn't yell, and doesn't grab the handlebars either. They jog alongside, say something encouraging, steady the seat for a second, and then, at the right moment, let go. That's almost exactly the shape of the next four steps in the breathing discourse. They're about the mind itself: getting to know it, cheering it up, steadying it, and finally, letting it go free.
screen: `A KID LEARNING TO RIDE.` → `ENCOURAGE, STEADY, LET GO.` → `FOUR STEPS FOR THE MIND.`

segments.voice: The third group of four is about citta, the mind or heart. Step nine: experiencing the mind, I will breathe in and out. Just knowing what state it's in right now: busy or quiet, dull or bright, tight or open. Step ten: gladdening the mind. If it's heavy or discouraged, you gently lift it. The old manual connects this with the gladness that comes as the mind settles; some teachers also suggest remembering something good, a kindness, a moment of calm, the qualities of the Buddha. Not fake cheer, just enough encouragement to keep going. Step eleven: steadying the mind, concentrating it. If it's scattered, you collect it on the breath, the way you'd gather loose papers into a neat stack. Step twelve: liberating the mind. The manual explains this as freeing the mind from whatever binds it in that moment: dullness, restlessness, grasping at a thought. Loosening the knot, one breath at a time. There's a real skill here: reading your own mind the way a good gardener reads the soil, and giving it what it needs. Sluggish? Brighten it. Scattered? Gather it. Caught? Let it go. That's not suppressing anything. It's care. And look back at this week: eleven blessings of kindness, then the breath in sixteen steps. Long and short. The whole body. Joy and ease. The weather of the mind. And now, the mind gladdened and released. Twelve of the sixteen steps. Tomorrow, the last four.
screen: `STEP NINE: KNOW THE MIND.` · `STEP TEN: GLADDEN IT.` · `STEP ELEVEN: STEADY IT.` · `STEP TWELVE: SET IT FREE.` · then, large: `RELEASE.`

segments.voice: Notice what your mind is like right now. If it feels heavy, bring to mind one good thing from today and let it brighten you a little; if it's scattered, count a few breaths to gather it; if it's gripping a thought, feel the grip and loosen it on the out-breath, like opening a fist. Then rest with the breath.

Your line: release. Know it, lift it, steady it, then let it go free. That's the week, and day one hundred and twelve.

fork.reveal: a heavy mind is gently gladdened first: remember something good, and let it brighten you.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: mind, heart; the third tetrad of the breathing discourse is about citta.

trapdoor: what you thought: cheer up.
what it means: reading the mind and giving it what it needs: brighten it, gather it, loosen it.
what a scholar hears: steps nine to twelve form the cittanupassana tetrad of MN 118; the Visuddhimagga explains vimocayam as freeing the mind from the hindrances and from wrong perceptions.

sources.ref: MN 118, Anapanasati Sutta: steps nine to twelve
